items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I gave him the Steve Allen and Regis Philbins and Don Rickles and the Milton Berles, and all the things I had something to do with my television experience.

ctx.x: And the first chapter has been sent in. I gave them the television chapter because they know I’m a jazz musician, there’ll be a lot about jazz musicians, and I gave him the Steve Allen and Regis Philbins and Don Rickles and the Milton Berles, and all the things I had something to do with my television experience. So they liked it. Now when I get back, I’m writing with a gentleman called Cary Ginell, who produced an NPR show, a Nancy Wilson thing, for my 75th birthday. And he’s editing the thing with me. So we…
names. But I can talk about it now. Because I look for humor in everything. Things that weren’t funny then, I can look now and they were funny but tragic at the same time.

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I became Don Rickles when I was on stage.

ctx.x: You know what, Monk? That part of your life you never thought about because that was part of getting on the bandstand. That led up to getting dressed, showered, changed, whatever. There were some times when we drove 500 miles and I did all the drive — I was the leader, I was the band boy, I used to load up the instruments because I knew we had to place them in the trunk. We had two cars. I had a Cadillac which in those days you could buy it for four thousand, five thousand dollars. And I had what they call a…

having fun. Me having fun. The audience had fun because we were having fun. You know it’s very infectious. But when I got onstage I always — ‘cause I love clubs. I hate concerts. I hate big — playing at the Playboy Festival was the most money I ever made for a job, but the audience is twenty feet away, the closest person. There’s no rapport with anybody. I get on stage first, and I make sure the band, we have fun. You can talk, you know, you’ve got something stupid, silly, I’m the best straight man you ever had,…

Well I’m going to turn to the book of Gibbs here, because it reminded me of something that I circled. And you wrote, “ For most musicians playing music is a crutch. If you have nothing else happening in your life at least you know you can play music. Things are bad for whatever reason, your wife left you, you’re not making any money, you can’t pay the mortgage, you can always pick up your horn and play. It gives you something that you can’t buy.”
